headline: Still a landlord's market despite quarterly rent flatline; re-acceleration of rent growth likely as investor pullback threatens future rental supply
reasoning: Nicola Powell argues that while rents flatlined over the September quarter, this may simply reflect seasonal effects rather than a structural easing. She highlights that investor behaviour has shifted significantly in response to budget changes to investment property taxation, with ABS home loan lending data showing investors pulling back. This reduced investor participation threatens future rental supply, which she expects will pressure vacancy rates and could re-ignite rent growth. She also notes the fastest and deepest downturns on record (30 years of data) in Sydney and Melbourne property prices, which further erodes investor confidence given weakening capital growth. She concludes it remains a rental crisis and that the full impacts of the tax changes have yet to be felt.
quote: I think this is the area that does concern us moving forward because we know that those budget changes came at a time we're already seeing a cyclical slowdown in our housing market. And you know we saw structural changes come head first colliding with that cyclical slowdown. So you know when you're looking at the downturn, we saw the shop is start to a downturn in Sydney and Melbourne that we've seen in on record which is 30 years of of price data for us. I think investor behaviour has shifted significantly. Investors are uncertain, they're cautious. Even when you look at ABS home loan lending, we know that investors have pulled back and that is going to affect future rental supply. So I think we are still concerned that we haven't actually seen the full impacts of that changes to the way in which we tax investment property. I think investors are going to still be that that buyer cohort that pull back and particularly with capital growth in, you know book prices falling and I think that is going to impact future rental supplies. So time's going to tell. I think we've still got a landlord's market. This is still a rental crisis and we're concerned what that means for ongoing future supply of rental properties.

headline: Mum-and-dad landlords under pressure from higher rates; some forced sales expected but distressed listings remain very low
reasoning: Powell highlights that most Australian rental stock is owned by individual investors holding a single property, who remain cost-sensitive amid high inflation and rising cash rates. Servicing and holding rental debt is becoming more painful and further rate rises are anticipated. Some investors may be forced to sell, but Powell expects cost-cutting to precede distress, meaning outright forced or urgent sales will remain limited. First home buyers in low-equity, affordable suburbs such as Blacktown in Sydney are the most vulnerable cohort for distressed listings, though the overall distress proportion remains very low.
quote: I think it is challenging. I think what we have to remember is that most of the rental stock in Australia is provided by mum and dad investors and a large pool of them are just people who own one rental property. These are families, they are households that are still cost sensitive as well. We've still got high levels of inflation. We've seen the cash rate move higher, which means that servicing and holding that debt is going to be more painful and we're still expecting the cash rate to move further again. So I think there will be some investors that will have to sell off and choose to offload their properties as a result of the higher costs.

headline: Housing unaffordability forcing young adults to stay home longer, driving behavioural shifts toward house-sharing and cheaper locations
reasoning: Powell notes that renters are exhibiting significant behavioural change in response to high rent prices, seeking more affordable locations, different property types, house shares, and room rentals. The intergenerational report recently released shows young adults staying at home for longer periods, which she views as a direct indicator of the depth of the affordability crisis. The inability to afford renting or purchasing a first home is reshaping life-stage transitions at a demographic level.
quote: You know, it plays out in behavioural change. They look towards different locations, different property types in order to cost cut and particularly in the rental space, you see people renting out a room or going into a house share. And I think some of the interesting demographic shifts that we're seeing and life stages changing. You know, the intergenerational report that was released recently shows that young adults are staying at home for much longer periods of time. And I think that really highlights the the face of affordability that we've got today is that it is unaffordable to move out of home and rent or even edge to towards purchasing your first time.

headline: Rental growth flatlining across capital cities despite tight vacancy rates, as affordability limits cap how much renters can absorb further hikes
reasoning: Nicola Powell notes that most capital cities saw rents flatline over the September quarter, with Sydney houses and Canberra houses recording marginal falls. Despite very low vacancy rates — which historically drive rental growth — affordability limits have been reached by tenants, constraining further rent increases. The September quarter is also seasonally weaker for rental growth. Powell expects the real test to come at the seasonal changeover period towards year end. Darwin was the notable exception, with strong house rent growth driven by the tightest vacancy rate of all capital cities.
quote: It is quite unusual. We saw most of our capital cities flatline over the September quarter. And actually we saw Sydney Houses and Canberra Houses fall over the September quarter only marginally, but it was still a full. And this is really unusual because what we still have is very tight vacancy rates, very low vacancy rates across all of our major capital cities. And normally when you do have low vacancy rates, it does translate into rental growth and that's not what we're seeing. I think it's a couple of factors. I think affordability limits have been reached by tenants and I think that's limiting how much rents can move higher and how much pass through of rental price hikes tenants can actually absorb.

headline: Renters adapting via behavioural change — different locations, house-shares, staying home longer — as unaffordability reshapes demographic life stages
reasoning: Powell describes how renters facing large rent hikes increasingly seek more affordable alternatives through location changes, different property types, room rentals or house shares. She also points to the intergenerational report showing young adults staying in the family home for longer periods, which she sees as a direct reflection of today's affordability challenge — it is unaffordable both to rent independently and to make a first property purchase. This demographic shift has been playing out in the rental market for some time.
quote: I think that dynamic has been unravelling in now rental space for some time. I think when you look at the rental market, it is more transient. And what that means is when you are faced with a strong rent price hike, you start to look for more affordable alternatives. And we're seeing that play out. You know, it plays out in behavioural change. They look towards different locations, different property types in order to cost cut and particularly in the rental space, you see people renting out a room or going into a house share. And I think some of the interesting demographic shifts that we're seeing and life stages changing. You know, the intergenerational report that was released recently shows that young adults are staying at home for much longer periods of time. And I think that really highlights the face of affordability that we've got today is that it is unaffordable to move out of home and rent or even edge towards purchasing your first time.
